summary: Selene Horizon helps mission planners pick a Moon south pole landing site that will not die in the dark. It compares six real NASA Artemis III candidate regions using horizons ray-cast from real LOLA terrain data, with Sun and Earth positions verified against NASA JPL Horizons (13,044 checks; Sun within 0.080°, Earth within 0.464°). For every site it computes live sunlight, Earth visibility, longest darkness, shadowed-region distance and surface temperature — then gives a clear verdict. Real data. Real geometry. Computed live.
details:
What it does: Selene Horizon is a lunar landing site browser for NASA's CLPS / Artemis III era. It compares six real candidate landing regions near the Moon's south pole — Shackleton Connecting Ridge, Shackleton Crater Rim, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton Plateau, Faustini Rim A and de Gerlache Rim — and answers the two questions that decide whether a lander lives or dies: how much sunlight will it get for power, and how often can it see Earth to communicate?

How it works: For each site, a 360° horizon profile is ray-cast from real Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data, so hills that block the Sun or Earth are the actual terrain, not an approximation. Sun and Earth positions are computed continuously and were verified against NASA's JPL Horizons ephemeris across 13,044 hourly and daily checks for 2026 (maximum error: Sun 0.080°, Earth 0.464°). On top of this the app computes annual and 30-day sunlight percentage, longest continuous darkness, Earth-visibility windows, distance to permanently shadowed regions (PGDA data), Diviner surface temperatures, and a 7-day battery and thermal survival model. A live "NOW" strip shows which sites are in sunlight at this moment, with ticking countdowns to the next sunrise, sunset or Earth contact.

Benefits and impact: Professional tools for this analysis exist, but their interfaces are built for specialists. Selene Horizon presents the same real data in plain English with a clear computed verdict, so mission planners can shortlist sites quickly, CLPS providers can sanity-check a target region, and educators and the public can genuinely understand why the south pole is hard: darkness can last two weeks, shadowed ground drops below −200°C, and Earth can hide below the horizon for weeks.

Tools and technology: React, TypeScript and Vite; NASA LOLA, LROC, Diviner, LEND and LAMP data via the Planetary Data System and PGDA; JPL Horizons for ephemeris verification; an automated test suite (37 tests) plus an in-app data-integrity audit. The app was developed with AI assistance (Google AI Studio / Gemini and Claude), declared in the SI section.

Creativity and factors considered: Each site is presented as a landed device with live status, countdowns and a 60-second guided Judge Mode tour. Site selection weighs the real trade-offs planners face: a ridge with near-constant sunlight may sit far from shadowed ice, while a site near ice may endure longer darkness — the comparison view makes that trade-off visible instead of hiding it in tables.
